title: Always test explicit names with name predicate when ignore unavailable

timeline.message: Always use predicate for explicit name check
timeline.author: Albert Zaharovits

timeline.body:
### Background

The Security filter rewrites requests to remove some **non-wildcard** names
when the `ignore_unavailable` request option is `true`. See: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/3fd338ffd15d7d7cafc15b6405d11e64a4641225/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/cluster/metadata/IndexAbstractionResolver.java#L103 and https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/995f578d83970d85df9fd41838a8b5c4e69dfb77/x-pack/plugin/security/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/security/authz/RBACEngine.java#L785

It **must** remove unauthorized names.
But it doesn't have to remove **authorized** names that:
 * are datastreams, in case the request doesn't handle datastreams (Core code ignores such datastreams already)
 * are backing indices of datastreams in case the request doesn't handle datastreams and the user only has permissions on the datastream, rather than on the index itself (it is probably a bug that such indices are currently removed)
 * are missing (Core code ignores missing names already, and removing them on the Security filter is causing the bug described here https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/90215)


### Proposal

Only remove **unauthorized** explicit names (existing or not) when `ignore_unavailable` is `true`,
in the Security filter, and leave the other explicit names, which are authorized, to be processed on
the Core side.

The first step towards that, which is what this PR does, is to always apply the "is-authorized" predicate
on the explicit names, rather than, in some cases, verify that the explicit name is among the
**existing** and authorized indices subset.

timeline.body: @ reviewers if you're on board with the proposed approach above, the next step is to discuss how the "is-authorized" predicate should look like. The PR at https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/91557 tries to change the current "is-authorized" predicate to address the issues, but I think a better option would be to straight up reuse the `IndicesPermission#isActionGranted` , though that would require some more refactoring...
Pinging @elastic/es-security (Team:Security)

I'm having a hard time connecting the dots between this PR and the proposal. On the surface it seems that this PR is just just removing an optimization (i.e. if we have fully resolved the supplier then just use the inner set as a cache to avoid work when checking for contains an item/collection ), so I am having a hard time seeing how the lack of optimization leads into a desired functional change. 

Also it is difficult to trace back to where all we call the contains/containsAll method to determine the impact of the removal of the optimization.

@jakelandis 

> where all we call the contains/containsAll method to determine the impact of the removal of the optimization.

The `contains` method is called at
https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/e68e28e4cb983cf06be5612b38078bc7d9e02f48/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/cluster/metadata/IndexAbstractionResolver.java#L103

The `containsAll` method is never used. It is included mainly for the `Set` interface.

For pure performance reason, I don't think we should remove the optimisation. The predicate is most likley more expensive since it internally has a `Map.get` call and a few other things. So it's going to be slower.

But I think @albertzaharovits needs it for the proposal here because the internal `authorizedIndices` set only contains authorized names that **exist** in the cluster state. It does *not* contain names that are authorized but absent from the cluster state (the absence could be temprorary because the index is being recovered). So the difference is that `authorizedIndices.contains` will return `false`, but `predicate.test` will return `true` for such index name. This subtle difference is what causing the issue in #90215.

Though this change will fix the specific issue of #90215, I feel it is a bit too obscure. It breaks the contract of the `Set` interface, i.e. `contains` returns `true`, but neither `iterator` nor `size` includes such element. That is weird at least. It also does not help when the request index name is a wildcard (e.g. `.kibana*`). The perfomance implication may not be much, but I cannot be sure either. Is it blocking your other work? If not, we may choose to defer it and look at it again once larger scale restructure is done?

> > I'm having a hard time connecting the dots between this PR and the proposal. On the surface it seems that this PR is just just removing an optimization (i.e. if we have fully resolved the supplier then just use the inner set as a cache to avoid work when checking for contains an item/collection ), so I am having a hard time seeing how the lack of optimization leads into a desired functional change.

> I think @albertzaharovits needs it for the proposal here because the internal authorizedIndices set only contains authorized names that exist in the cluster state. It does not contain names that are authorized but absent from the cluster state (the absence could be temprorary because the index is being recovered). So the difference is that authorizedIndices.contains will return false, but predicate.test will return true for such index name. This subtle difference is what causing the issue in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/90215.

What Yang says. The proposal is to "Only remove unauthorized explicit names", but the optimization that this PR takes away makes it that unauthorized **or missing** explicit names are removed. The optimisation is incompatible with the bug fix proposal.

> For pure performance reason, I don't think we should remove the optimisation. The predicate is most likley more expensive since it internally has a Map.get call and a few other things. So it's going to be slower.

I think it's worth pointing out that the predicate is only evaluated for explicit names. In general I think a performance penalty on the order of the explicit names in the request is not something we should worry about too much. Moreover, this inneficiency pales in comparison, to the check in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/e68e28e4cb983cf06be5612b38078bc7d9e02f48/x-pack/plugin/core/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/core/security/authz/permission/IndicesPermission.java#L510 which runs AGAIN on the explicit names, and the results from wildcard expansions.

> Though this change will fix the specific issue of https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/90215, I feel it is a bit too obscure. It breaks the contract of the Set interface, i.e. contains returns true, but neither iterator nor size includes such element.

I agree. I think the `AuthorizedIndices` class should not implement the `Set` interface anymore. I can implement this if you consent.

> It also does not help when the request index name is a wildcard (e.g. .kibana*).

True, but I think this has been acknowledged https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/90215#issuecomment-1273249327 (last line: "Make the Security filter NOT remove authorized names for missing indices when ignore_unavailable=true; this will fix this bug issue specifically, but if instead the request used wildcards rather than explicit names, it would still be possible to erroneously report that no such indices exist when in fact the cluster state is not yet recovered.")

> Is it blocking your other work? If not, we may choose to defer it and look at it again once larger scale restructure is done?

It blocks fixing a bug that I'm assigned to, which I don't know how to fix otherwise, and which I think makes ES appear inconsistent (so it's pretty serious), though the circumstances are particular (require usage of service account tokens).
It doesn't block the indices expression resolver refactoring.

> Btw, since we are aming to have a single implementation between core and security, have you considered how to unify them (different behaviours for ignore_unavailable on explicit names) when the time comes? I guess it can be parameterized? Or something else?

I hope in the end the method from Core will be parameterized, and called by the Security filter. The handling of explicit names is completely different in Security, and to make it easier to observe, I endeavor to pull it out of the wildcard resolver.

-[[speed_up_sql_queries_by_not_tracking_total_hits_by_default]]
-=== Speed up SQL queries by not tracking total hits by default
-SQL query translator now explicitly sets track_total_hits to false when
-not needed.
-This has a significant impact on SQL query performance in cases where total hits
-are not needed to calculate the final result, in particular when the cost of evaluation
-of a single document is particularly high (eg. queries that involve script evaluation)
-and in queries with a small LIMIT value.
-In our tests, on some specific queries, we see a speed-up of more than 50%,
-with peaks of ~95% (from 600ms to 20ms).
-
-{es-pull}89106[#89106]
-
-[discrete]
-[[ilm_no_longer_rolls_over_empty_indices]]
-=== ILM no longer rolls over empty indices
-For both new and existing Index Lifecycle Management (ILM) policies,
-the rollover action will only execute if an index has at least one document.
-
-
-For indices with a `max_age` condition that are no longer being written
-to, this will mean that they will no longer roll over every time their
-`max_age` is reached.
-
-A policy can override this behavior, and explicitly opt in to rolling over
-empty indices, by adding a `"min_docs": 0` condition:
-
-[source,console]
-----
-PUT _ilm/policy/allow_empty_rollover_policy
-{
-  "policy": {
-    "phases": {
-      "hot": {
-        "actions": {
-          "rollover" : {
-            "max_age": "7d",
-            "max_size": "100gb",
-            "min_docs": 0
-          }
-        }
-      }
-    }
-  }
-}
-----
-
-This can also be disabled on a cluster-wide basis by setting
-`indices.lifecycle.rollover.only_if_has_documents` to `false`.
-
-{es-pull}89557[#89557]
-
-[discrete]
-[[release_time_series_data_stream_tsds_functionality]]
-=== Release time series data stream (TSDS) functionality
-Elasticsearch offers support for time series data stream (TSDS) indices.
-A TSDS index is an index that contains time series metrics data as part
-of a data stream. Elasticsearch routes the incoming documents into a TSDS
-index so that all the documents for a particular time series are on the
-same shard, and then sorts the shard by time series and timestamp. This
-structure has a few advantages:
-
-1. Documents from the same time series are next to each other on the shard, and
-hence stored next to each other on the disk, so the operating system pages are
-much more homogeneous and compress better, yielding massive reduction in TCO.
-
-2. The analysis of a time series typically involves comparing each two consecutive
-docs (samples), examining the last doc in a given time window, etc., which is quite
-complex when the next doc could be on any shard, and in fact on any index. Sorting
-by time series and timestamp allows improved analysis, both in terms of performance
-and in terms of our ability to add new aggregations.
-
-Finally,  as part of the Index Lifecycle Management of metrics data time series,
-Elasticsearch enables a Downsampling action. When an index is downsampled,
-Elasticsearch keeps a single document with statistical summaries per each bucket
-of time in the time series. Supported aggregations can then be run on the data
-stream and include both downsampled indices and raw data indices, without the
-user needing to be aware of that. Downsampling of downsampled indices, to more
-coarse time resolution, is also supported.

+            #!/usr/local/bin/runbld --redirect-stderr
+            WORKFLOW="staging"

+            ES_VERSION=$(cat build-tools-internal/version.properties \

+            set +x
+            VAULT_TOKEN=$(vault write -field=token auth/approle/login role_id=$VAULT_ROLE_ID secret_id=$VAULT_SECRET_ID)
+            LICENSE_KEY=$(mktemp -d)/license.key
+            export VAULT_TOKEN
+            vault read -field pubkey secret/elasticsearch-ci/license | base64 --decode > $LICENSE_KEY
+            unset VAULT_TOKEN
+
+            $WORKSPACE/.ci/scripts/run-gradle.sh -Ddra.artifacts=true \

+
+            # Allow other users access to read the artifacts so they are readable in the
+            # container
+            find $WORKSPACE -type f -path "*/build/distributions/*" -exec chmod a+r {} \;

+            # Allow other users write access to create checksum files
+            find $WORKSPACE -type d -path "*/build/distributions" -exec chmod a+w {} \;
+
+            # Artifacts should be generated

+                   --name release-manager \
+                   -e VAULT_ADDR \
+                   -e VAULT_ROLE_ID \
+                   -e VAULT_SECRET_ID \
+                   --mount type=bind,readonly=false,src="$PWD",target=/artifacts \

-[[speed_up_sql_queries_by_not_tracking_total_hits_by_default]]
-=== Speed up SQL queries by not tracking total hits by default
-SQL query translator now explicitly sets track_total_hits to false when
-not needed.
-This has a significant impact on SQL query performance in cases where total hits
-are not needed to calculate the final result, in particular when the cost of evaluation
-of a single document is particularly high (eg. queries that involve script evaluation)
-and in queries with a small LIMIT value.
-In our tests, on some specific queries, we see a speed-up of more than 50%,
-with peaks of ~95% (from 600ms to 20ms).
-
-{es-pull}89106[#89106]
-
-[discrete]
-[[ilm_no_longer_rolls_over_empty_indices]]
-=== ILM no longer rolls over empty indices
-For both new and existing Index Lifecycle Management (ILM) policies,
-the rollover action will only execute if an index has at least one document.
-
-
-For indices with a `max_age` condition that are no longer being written
-to, this will mean that they will no longer roll over every time their
-`max_age` is reached.
-
-A policy can override this behavior, and explicitly opt in to rolling over
-empty indices, by adding a `"min_docs": 0` condition:
-
-[source,console]
-----
-PUT _ilm/policy/allow_empty_rollover_policy
-{
-  "policy": {
-    "phases": {
-      "hot": {
-        "actions": {
-          "rollover" : {
-            "max_age": "7d",
-            "max_size": "100gb",
-            "min_docs": 0
-          }
-        }
-      }
-    }
-  }
-}
-----
-
-This can also be disabled on a cluster-wide basis by setting
-`indices.lifecycle.rollover.only_if_has_documents` to `false`.
-
-{es-pull}89557[#89557]
-
-[discrete]
-[[release_time_series_data_stream_tsds_functionality]]
-=== Release time series data stream (TSDS) functionality
-Elasticsearch offers support for time series data stream (TSDS) indices.
-A TSDS index is an index that contains time series metrics data as part
-of a data stream. Elasticsearch routes the incoming documents into a TSDS
-index so that all the documents for a particular time series are on the
-same shard, and then sorts the shard by time series and timestamp. This
-structure has a few advantages:
-
-1. Documents from the same time series are next to each other on the shard, and
-hence stored next to each other on the disk, so the operating system pages are
-much more homogeneous and compress better, yielding massive reduction in TCO.
-
-2. The analysis of a time series typically involves comparing each two consecutive
-docs (samples), examining the last doc in a given time window, etc., which is quite
-complex when the next doc could be on any shard, and in fact on any index. Sorting
-by time series and timestamp allows improved analysis, both in terms of performance
-and in terms of our ability to add new aggregations.
-
-Finally,  as part of the Index Lifecycle Management of metrics data time series,
-Elasticsearch enables a Downsampling action. When an index is downsampled,
-Elasticsearch keeps a single document with statistical summaries per each bucket
-of time in the time series. Supported aggregations can then be run on the data
-stream and include both downsampled indices and raw data indices, without the
-user needing to be aware of that. Downsampling of downsampled indices, to more
-coarse time resolution, is also supported.
-

timeline.body:
It's a bit weird to wrap the normal supplier in a checked supplier where the checked exception type is a RuntimeException.  

I don't think any of the usage actually use checked suppliers with checked exceptions, so I am pretty sure we can change LazyInitializable to only accept the non-checked variety of suppliers.  I haven't tested...but [here is an example](https://github.com/jakelandis/elasticsearch/commit/a283b0c1689ba6a1dff4e80ece53d41278fed7a0) of changing  LazyInitializable to only support normal suppliers. I only confirmed it compiles. 

Probably more of a follow up rather than this with this PR, but I only looked at because I was originally confused by this.

reply.body: I've ended up replacing the `LazyInitializable` with a `CachedSupplier`, because `CachedSupplier` implements the `Supplier` interface which I've used in the method signature (because the "lazy" trait is an implementation detail).

timeline.body:
The changes here look good. I like the use of LazyInitializable to wrap the set instead of implementing the set interface for reasons previous discussed and the unique type makes it is easier to track the usages of when/where it used and fully resolved or not. 

However, maybe I am just confused (this all very complex), but I am still not fully understanding how this change fixes the initialization issue. 

> because the internal authorizedIndices set only contains authorized names that exist in the cluster state. It does not contain names that are authorized but absent from the cluster state (the absence could be temprorary because the index is being recovered). So the difference is that authorizedIndices.contains will return false, but predicate.test will return true for such index name. 

I don't see how the fully resolved set (i.e. allAuthorizedAndAvailable.getOrCompute()) would ever differ from singular predicate check (isAuthorized.test)). In both cases the index must be present in the view of cluster state to prevent it from being removed from the view that core will see. Both cases (full set / singular predicate) use the same view of the cluster state. When looking at the fully resolved set, the index will only be included in the results iff it is found in cluster state. When looking at the singular predicate, it will be only return true if the it is found in the cluster state (we explicitly look up the name and [return false](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/security/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/security/authz/RBACEngine.java#L788) if not found.)  So I guess I don't understand how this change influences what will be presented to core vs. not.

> I don't see how the fully resolved set (i.e. allAuthorizedAndAvailable.getOrCompute()) would ever differ from singular predicate check (isAuthorized.test)). In both cases the index must be present in the view of cluster state to prevent it from being removed from the view that core will see. Both cases (full set / singular predicate) use the same view of the cluster state. When looking at the fully resolved set, the index will only be included in the results iff it is found in cluster state. When looking at the singular predicate, it will be only return true if the it is found in the cluster state (we explicitly look up the name and [return false](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/security/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/security/authz/RBACEngine.java#L788) if not found.) So I guess I don't understand how this change influences what will be presented to core vs. not.

I think @jakelandis is absolutely right on this point. The predicate internally relies on the same cluster state view. As such, it won't give a different answer. I glossed over this important detail 🤦 It also shows that we need new tests for the change.

This might be a deal breaker ... Trying to work around it would lead to many cascading changes. It also has to ignore data stream (this reminds me that our index authorization is no longer purely string based). The benefit feels small compare to the complexities and compromises[^1]. It makes me retreat to my previous position of deferring it. Maybe I can be convinced again if there are creative ways to make it work. For now, this looks hard to converge because the fundamental underlying issue is security filter changes the order of execution for index resolving. What we are trying to have is an edge case point solution while the larger problem remains. The "alias pointing to closed index" problem can also be attributed to this overall issue. I wonder whether our long term goal is still have security filter plug into core (sorry I lost track on this)? If so, that might be the actual solution to this. But it is very hard change by itself, so I am not sure whether we can rely on that either. Sorry for the back and forth. This is more conflicting than I expected. I am willing to hear out other opinions. Thanks!

[^1]: It does not work with wildcards and probably not with explicit names matching backing indices either. > > I don't see how the fully resolved set (i.e. allAuthorizedAndAvailable.getOrCompute()) would ever differ from singular predicate check (isAuthorized.test)). In both cases the index must be present in the view of cluster state to prevent it from being removed from the view that core will see. Both cases (full set / singular predicate) use the same view of the cluster state. When looking at the fully resolved set, the index will only be included in the results iff it is found in cluster state. When looking at the singular predicate, it will be only return true if the it is found in the cluster state (we explicitly look up the name and [return false](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/security/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/security/authz/RBACEngine.java#L788) if not found.) So I guess I don't understand how this change influences what will be presented to core vs. not.

> I think @jakelandis is absolutely right on this point. The predicate internally relies on the same cluster state view. As such, it won't give a different answer. I glossed over this important detail 🤦 It also shows that we need new tests for the change.

This PR is not a fix for the bug! From the PR description:
> The first step towards that, which is what this PR does, is to always apply the "is-authorized" predicate
on the explicit names, rather than, in some cases, verify that the explicit name is among the
existing and authorized indices subset.

The predicate must be changed for the PR to be fixed. But this is going to be a follow-up PR. And that PR is going to be labeled `bug-fix` . And before that I was going to raise a discuss issue because there are two options for the new predicate that I would need your input to evaluate.
This PR is just a starting point. Look at the initial commit, from the version I initially asked review of: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/91618/commits/1a3e6479f31c6a80982c6cc0589301a77270f714 . How could have that change fixed the bug? The predicate test and the set test are equivalent today, otherwise the current code in `main` would be broken. I need to get this PR merged first, because I cannot change the predicate and keep the authorized set logic the same, because the is authorized check of "sometimes check set contains sometimes evaluate predicate" would be broken. 

Should we set a sync discussion to clarify the scope of this PR?

> This might be a deal breaker ... Trying to work around it would lead to many cascading changes. It also has to ignore data stream (this reminds me that our index authorization is no longer purely string based). The benefit feels small compare to the complexities and compromises[1](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/91618#user-content-fn-1-b689671c263724328c022f7a714f8624). It makes me retreat to my previous position of deferring it. Maybe I can be convinced again if there are creative ways to make it work. For now, this looks hard to converge because the fundamental underlying issue is security filter changes the order of execution for index resolving. What we are trying to have is an edge case point solution while the larger problem remains. The "alias pointing to closed index" problem can also be attributed to this overall issue. I wonder whether our long term goal is still have security filter plug into core (sorry I lost track on this)? If so, that might be the actual solution to this. But it is very hard change by itself, so I am not sure whether we can rely on that either. Sorry for the back and forth. This is more conflicting than I expected. I am willing to hear out other opinions. Thanks!

I'm sorry but I don't understand what is the newly discovered issue that is a deal-breaker here. I will propose we have a sync conv.

Yang and I had a chat before in the day on this topic. Here are my take aways from the conversation:

* this PR is not a bug fix, it is only a refactoring
* we need to discuss on the "is authorized" predicate, used in the request expression rewriting, in order to fix the bug in #90215
* the new predicate will have to work on `String`s too (for missing indices), very similarly to how the `IndicesPermission#isActionGranted` test works
* I should change the method signature for `AuthorizationEngine#AuthorizedIndices#allAuthorizedAndAvailable` back to return a `Supplier<Set<String>>`, because the lazy trait is an implementation detail and the lack of thread-safetiness is not a concern

timeline.body: Nit: Can we renamed the variable to `authorizedIndices`? The existing name `list` is rather confusing after this refactor. The same comment applies to two other methods (`testDataStreamsAreNotIncludedInAuthorizedIndices`, `testDataStreamsAreIncludedInAuthorizedIndices`) in this test class as well.
Nit: This assertion is not necessary anymore since the AuthorizedIndices is no longer a Set implementation and the type is guaranteed statically.
Same here. The assertion is not needed anymore.

LGTM Thanks for working through this and providing clarification along the way. 

The `CustomAuthorizationEngine` needs to be updated once this PR is merged.

This is an idea for possible future refactoring (no need to do anything for this PR): I like the new `AuthorizedIndices` interface. It is rather unfortunate that it has to be decomposed into two parameters when it is used with `IndexAbstractionResolver`. The main reason is because `IndexAbstractionResolver` is in core. But does it have to be? As far as I can tell, it is only used by `ResolveIndexAction`. Everything else in core uses `IndexNameExpressionResolver`. Is there anything special about `ResolveIndexAction` to justify it being different? If not, we could replace its usage and move `IndexAbstractionResolver` to xpack. This way, we can not only use the `AuthorizedIndices` interface everywhere but also likely be able to improve the interface to enforce its internal consistency, i.e. all names from the supplier should pass `check`, but not the other way around. We could even choose to hide the `Supplier` usage so that `AuthorizedIndices#all` simply returns a `Set`.

+/**
+ *
+ * Wraps an async action that consumes an {@link ActionListener} such that multiple invocations of {@link #execute(ActionListener)} can
+ * share the result from a single call to the wrapped action. This implementation is similar to {@link ResultDeduplicator} but offers
+ * stronger guarantees of not seeing a stale result ever. Concretely, every invocation of {@link #execute(ActionListener)} is guaranteed to
+ * be resolved with a response that has been computed at a time after the call to {@code execute} has been made. This allows this class to
+ * be used to deduplicate results from actions that produce results that change over time transparently.
+ *
+ * @param <T> Result type
+ */
+public final class SingleResultDeduplicator<T> {
+
+    private final ThreadContext threadContext;
+
+    /**
+     * List of listeners waiting for the execution after the current in-progress execution. If {@code null} then no execution is in
+     * progress currently, otherwise an execution is in progress and will trigger another execution that will resolve any listeners queued
+     * up here once done.
+     */
+    private List<ActionListener<T>> waitingListeners;
+
+    private final Consumer<ActionListener<T>> executeAction;
+
+    public SingleResultDeduplicator(ThreadContext threadContext, Consumer<ActionListener<T>> executeAction) {
+        this.threadContext = threadContext;
+        this.executeAction = executeAction;
+    }
+
+    /**
+     * Execute the action for the given {@code listener}.
+     * @param listener listener to resolve with execution result
+     */
+    public void execute(ActionListener<T> listener) {
+        synchronized (this) {
+            if (waitingListeners == null) {
+                // no queued up listeners, just execute this one directly without deduplication and instantiate the list so that
+                // subsequent executions will wait
+                waitingListeners = new ArrayList<>();
+            } else {
+                // already running an execution, queue this one up
+                waitingListeners.add(ContextPreservingActionListener.wrapPreservingContext(listener, threadContext));
+                return;
+            }
+        }
+        doExecute(listener);
+    }
+
+    private void doExecute(ActionListener<T> listener) {
+        final ActionListener<T> wrappedListener = ActionListener.runBefore(listener, () -> {
+            final List<ActionListener<T>> listeners;
+            synchronized (this) {
+                if (waitingListeners.isEmpty()) {
+                    // no listeners were queued up while this execution ran, so we just reset the state to not having a running execution
+                    waitingListeners = null;
+                    return;
+                } else {
+                    // we have queued up listeners, so we create a fresh list for the next execution and execute once to handle the
+                    // listeners currently queued up
+                    listeners = waitingListeners;
+                    waitingListeners = new ArrayList<>();
+                }
+            }
+            doExecute(new ActionListener<>() {
+                @Override
+                public void onResponse(T response) {
+                    ActionListener.onResponse(listeners, response);
+                }
+
+                @Override
+                public void onFailure(Exception e) {
+                    ActionListener.onFailure(listeners, e);
+                }
+            });
+        });

+            executeAction.accept(wrappedListener);

+        }

+    public void testDeduplicatesWithoutShowingStaleData() {
+        final SetOnce<ActionListener<Object>> firstListenerRef = new SetOnce<>();
+        final SetOnce<ActionListener<Object>> secondListenerRef = new SetOnce<>();
+        final var deduplicator = new SingleResultDeduplicator<>(new ThreadContext(Settings.EMPTY), l -> {
+            if (firstListenerRef.trySet(l) == false) {
+                secondListenerRef.set(l);
+            }
+        });
+        final Object result1 = new Object();
+        final Object result2 = new Object();
+
+        final int totalListeners = randomIntBetween(2, 10);
+        final boolean[] called = new boolean[totalListeners];
+        deduplicator.execute(new ActionListener<>() {
+            @Override
+            public void onResponse(Object response) {
+                assertFalse(called[0]);
+                called[0] = true;
+                assertEquals(result1, response);
+            }
+
+            @Override
+            public void onFailure(Exception e) {
+                throw new AssertionError(e);
+            }
+        });
+
+        for (int i = 1; i < totalListeners; i++) {
+            final int index = i;
+            deduplicator.execute(new ActionListener<>() {
+
+                @Override
+                public void onResponse(Object response) {
+                    assertFalse(called[index]);
+                    called[index] = true;
+                    assertEquals(result2, response);
+                }
+
+                @Override
+                public void onFailure(Exception e) {
+                    throw new AssertionError(e);
+                }
+            });
+        }
+        for (int i = 0; i < totalListeners; i++) {
+            assertFalse(called[i]);
+        }
+        firstListenerRef.get().onResponse(result1);
+        assertTrue(called[0]);
+        for (int i = 1; i < totalListeners; i++) {
+            assertFalse(called[i]);
+        }
+        secondListenerRef.get().onResponse(result2);
+        for (int i = 0; i < totalListeners; i++) {
+            assertTrue(called[i]);
+        }
+    }

timeline.body:
>  I like the new AuthorizedIndices interface. It is rather unfortunate that it has to be decomposed into two parameters when it is used with IndexAbstractionResolver. The main reason is because IndexAbstractionResolver is in core. But does it have to be? As far as I can tell, it is only used by ResolveIndexAction. Everything else in core uses IndexNameExpressionResolver. Is there anything special about ResolveIndexAction to justify it being different? If not, we could replace its usage and move IndexAbstractionResolver to xpack.

There shouldn't be anything special about the `ResolveIndexAction` for it to use the Security's implementation (which confusingly is packaged in Core) of the resolver, i.e. the `IndexAbstractionResolver`; though I haven't looked closely.
In any case, the objective is to use a single implementation for the resolver, the one Core uses, i.e. `org.elasticsearch.cluster.metadata.IndexNameExpressionResolver`. I'll hold off refactoring the `IndexAbstractionResolver` because it's very likely to be removed soon.

> The CustomAuthorizationEngine needs to be updated once this PR is merged.

Pushed [209f101](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/91618/commits/209f10118d4ae79503d475abb6d7790a03242206).

For posterity, the example plugins, of which `security-authorization-engine` is one instance, are not tested in PR CI tests.
They are tested in a separate periodic CI job:  https://elasticsearch-ci.elastic.co/job/elastic+elasticsearch+pull-request+example-plugins/ .

If anything about the `AuthorizationEngine` interface changes, almost always the plugin's implementation, i.e. `CustomAuthorizationEngine`, also needs to be adjusted. You can use the following command to compile the `security-authorization-engine` plugin `(cd plugins/examples && ./gradlew :security-authorization-engine:compileJava --include-build ../..)` ; I also had to set `org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g` to my `~/.gradle/gradle.properties` file in order to avoid `OutOfMemoryError`s during the build.
